title: Regenerate a severely damaged adult human heart

concept.text: The innovation would restore enough living, functioning heart muscle in a severely damaged adult human heart to produce durable improvement in its pumping ability. Newly formed or implanted muscle would need an adequate blood supply, sustained survival and functional coordination with the recipient heart. The intended achievement extends from replacing lost muscle to demonstrating that the repaired heart supports patients’ daily activities and long-term health.

Engineered heart muscle grafts provide one documented route. Stem-cell-derived heart muscle tissue is implanted onto the heart, where its retention, vascularization and contribution to contraction can be studied. The research also identifies reprogramming cells in place and stimulating existing heart cells as possible routes. These remain conceptual possibilities within this record because the supplied evidence does not assess their performance.

significance.text: Durable restoration of substantial, coordinated muscle would make an important component of severe heart damage repairable. The revolutionary capability would be to rebuild working myocardial tissue in an adult heart whose muscle loss has been treated as largely irreversible. The reported animal improvements in local heart-wall contraction and global pumping function provide a technical basis for pursuing this goal, while the magnitude and durability of benefit in patients remain open.

If regenerated muscle produced sustained clinical benefit, it could reduce the burden of heart failure, improve daily function and survival, and reduce patients’ need for transplantation or mechanical circulatory support. These outcomes require clinical demonstration. The supplied study’s bridge-to-transplant rationale illustrates a possible intermediate application in which added muscle supports a patient awaiting transplantation.

Synthesis of the proposed impact places practical limits on the regeneration analogy. Repairing lost myocardium would leave separate questions about ongoing disease, damage to other cardiac structures and the suitability of treatment for different patients. Extension to other organs would require advances specific to their cells, architecture and physiological functions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is durable restoration of enough vascularized, functionally coordinated muscle to substantially improve a severely damaged adult human heart with acceptable risks. The engineering problem includes retaining sufficient cardiomyocytes, supplying them with blood, achieving the maturation needed for sustained performance and maintaining their contribution over time. Retention alone leaves unresolved how much viable tissue is needed and how effectively it can augment a failing heart.

Functional coordination is the relevant requirement, while its necessary mechanism remains unsettled. The supplied study explains that epicardial tissue patches have difficulty forming conventional electromechanical connections through intercalated discs and proposes mechanical entrainment as a possible way they contribute to heart performance. That mechanism remains a hypothesis requiring further investigation. The degree of electrical coupling and tissue maturation needed for durable benefit may depend on the treatment approach.

Safety and durability barriers include dangerous arrhythmias, tumors or other abnormal tissue growth, immune rejection and deterioration of the restored muscle. Observed osteochondral differentiation makes control of unintended tissue formation a concrete concern. In the macaque work, graft retention depended on suitable immunosuppression, while other regimens and withdrawal produced rejection. A practical treatment must therefore establish both a reliable tissue product and an acceptable long-term immune-management strategy.

current_state.text: The Nature report by Ahmad-Fawad Jebran and colleagues, published on 29 January 2025, documented engineered heart muscle allografts in macaques and a human recipient. In macaques, graft cardiomyocytes were retained for up to six months under tacrolimus and methylprednisolone. Some treated animals in the heart-failure model showed improved target-wall contractility and ejection fraction, representing local and global measures of cardiac support. These findings establish preclinical remuscularization and functional support within the studied conditions.

The same report identified graft cardiomyocytes in one human heart explanted approximately three months after implantation, with graft identity confirmed through single-nucleotide variant analyses. The retained cells showed relative immaturity, lower capillary density and local immune-cell infiltration. This observation establishes human graft retention over that interval. Durable restoration of clinical function and benefit attributable to the graft remain to be demonstrated in controlled studies.

The research cites a subsequent report attributed to Wolfram-Hubertus Zimmermann and colleagues, titled “Stem-Cell–Derived Biologic Ventricular Assist Tissue in Heart Failure,” with a stated publication date of 27 May 2026. It attributes feasibility findings, short-term signals and serious adverse events, including deaths during follow-up, to that report. The supplied review found that the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie notice and provides neither an assessable abstract nor verified article identity. Those clinical findings and the publication metadata therefore remain unverified in this record. The research’s account of a publisher 403 response and a first-pass abstract review also lacks retained supporting material. This evidence gap leaves the report’s results open.

The evidence assessment above follows the supplied review. It reports substantive, complete saved HTML for the 2025 Nature article and an extractable protocol supplement. The main article’s PDF extraction was truncated, and a separate supplementary PDF had pages without extractable text. The reviewed textual findings support the animal and human-retention conclusions without requiring independent interpretation of the underlying images. The supplied freshness search record is empty, so completeness of the field assessment through 1 November 2026 remains unassessed.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstrations would combine evidence of substantial new functional myocardium with controlled evidence of durable patient benefit. Independent studies should reproduce the result and prespecify clinically meaningful benefit thresholds, follow-up duration and methods for establishing the restored tissue’s contribution to heart performance. The BioVAT-HF protocol provides relevant outcome categories, including structural and functional augmentation, functional status, patient-reported outcomes, mortality, arrhythmias and rejection. The broader completion criteria proposed here extend beyond that protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated demonstrations link new functional myocardium to durable patient benefit

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical criteria would require durable improvements in survival and daily function, together with reduced need for transplantation or mechanical support, across several causes of severe heart damage. Studies should establish which disease settings and patient groups benefit, the amount and location of muscle restoration required, and the treatment’s practical delivery and immune-management requirements. These are proposed evaluative criteria. Numerical thresholds and follow-up periods remain to be specified, and finite trials would establish the breadth demonstrated in their participants and conditions.
completion_criteria.label: Durable clinical benefits span several causes of severe heart damage

completion_criteria.text: Proposed long-term safety assessment would track arrhythmias, tumors, abnormal tissue formation, immune complications and durability of the restored muscle. Follow-up should be long enough to detect delayed loss of benefit or tissue-related complications, with sustained surveillance after the main trial. The supplied BioVAT-HF protocol’s proposed lifelong registry follow-up provides a relevant precedent for extended observation. Durability assessment should accommodate both graft-based treatments and any future approach that restores muscle within the heart.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained surveillance tracks restored muscle durability and delayed complications

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis connects CAR-01 with three other approaches to severe pump failure. CAR-03, a durable, broadly affordable total artificial heart, concerns mechanical replacement of pumping function. CAR-04, a dependable supply of transplantable animal hearts, concerns donor-organ replacement and its biological compatibility. CAR-07, a transplantable, fully engineered living human heart, overlaps strongly in tissue engineering, vascularization and maturation while adding the challenge of constructing a complete transplantable organ. CAR-01 focuses on restoring muscle within the recipient’s existing heart.

Roster-based synthesis links CAR-02, reliable reversal of advanced atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree, and CAR-12, detection of actionable coronary plaque risk before a first clinical event, to the vascular causes and prevention of cardiac injury. Their targets are arterial disease and risk identification. CAR-01 addresses restoration after severe myocardial damage. Success in either vascular concept could complement regeneration by reducing future injury, with the combined benefit requiring demonstration.

Roster-based synthesis distinguishes CAR-05, durable correction of inherited heart disease directly in the beating heart, from CAR-01’s tissue-restoration goal. Correcting an inherited cause and rebuilding muscle lost to disease could be complementary achievements. CAR-13, broad prevention of cardiac injury from cancer treatment without weakening cancer control, addresses prevention under an additional constraint on cancer outcomes. Its relationship to CAR-01 is the possibility of reducing the injury that would otherwise require repair.

Roster-based synthesis connects CAR-06, making most preventable sudden cardiac deaths predictable and preventable, and CAR-09, a durable, non-ablative cure for atrial fibrillation, through cardiac rhythm and electrical safety. Arrhythmia risk is an important constraint on muscle regeneration. Each related concept nevertheless has its own clinical endpoint, encompassing prediction and prevention of sudden death or durable control of atrial fibrillation.

Roster-based synthesis places CAR-08, durable reversal of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, alongside CAR-01 as a distinct heart-failure objective whose responsiveness to muscle restoration would require disease-specific evidence. CAR-10, reversal of established calcific aortic stenosis without valve replacement, targets valve disease. CAR-11, reversal of pulmonary arterial hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences, targets pulmonary vascular disease and its effects on the heart. Repairing myocardium could overlap with treatment of resulting cardiac damage, while each concept retains a separate underlying disease target.

unresolved_issues: The subsequent clinical report’s identity, publication metadata, feasibility results, short-term outcomes and serious adverse events require assessable retained source material.
The supplied evidence does not establish the performance of in-place reprogramming or stimulation of existing cells.
The mechanisms and degree of electrical coupling, mechanical coordination and maturation required for durable benefit remain unresolved.
The amount of restored muscle needed for clinically meaningful benefit, acceptable immune-management burden and long-term tissue durability remain to be established.
Numerical benefit thresholds, follow-up durations and the disease settings needed to satisfy the proposed completion criteria remain unspecified.
The empty freshness search record prevents an assessment of research completeness through 1 November 2026.
Some supplementary PDF pages lack extractable text, and the main article PDF extraction was truncated. Conclusions here follow the supplied review’s substantive HTML and assessed supplementary text.

brief.title: Rebuilding a severely damaged adult heart
possible: People with severely damaged hearts could regain lasting pumping strength by replacing lost heart muscle. The new muscle would stay alive, receive enough blood and work with the rest of the heart.
why: Rebuilding working muscle could make severe heart damage repairable. For people with heart failure, it could improve daily activities and survival, while reducing the need for a transplant or a mechanical pump.

sources.showed: Lab-grown heart muscle patches survived and developed a working blood supply in macaques. Some animals with heart failure showed stronger pumping. Implanted muscle also survived in a human recipient.
sources.quote:
Our clinical data confirmed remuscularization by 
EHM implantation in a patient with advanced heart failure.
sources.cited_for: The study supports replacing lost heart muscle with living patches and shows improved pumping in some treated animals.
sources.not_established: It did not establish lasting improvements in patients’ daily function or survival caused by the implanted muscle.

sources.who: Wolfram-Hubertus Zimmermann and the BioVAT-HF Investigators
sources.showed: An early trial treated 20 patients with lab-grown heart muscle patches. Follow-up found thicker heart walls and improved pumping measurements. All patients had adverse events, and some died.
sources.quote: All the patients had at least one adverse event.
sources.cited_for: The trial provides early human results for muscle patches, including changes in heart function and safety concerns.
sources.not_established: The trial lacked a comparison group and did not establish lasting benefit or how much improvement the patches caused.

shown: Ahmad-Fawad Jebran and colleagues kept implanted heart muscle alive in macaques for up to six months using medicines that suppress immune rejection. Some animals with heart failure showed improved pumping. The team also found surviving implanted muscle in a human heart.

Wolfram-Hubertus Zimmermann and colleagues reported improved pumping measurements after three months in an early human trial without a comparison group. Every participant had an adverse event, and deaths occurred during follow-up. Lasting patient benefit remains unproven.
missing: Controlled studies have yet to show that enough new, working muscle causes lasting improvements in patients’ health and daily activities.
Restored muscle must receive enough blood, mature and keep working with the heart over time.
Treatment must control dangerous heart rhythms, tumors, unintended tissue growth and immune rejection with an acceptable long-term treatment burden.

milestones.label: Independent studies link new muscle to lasting patient benefit
milestones.explanation: Independent controlled studies would have to link substantial new working heart muscle to lasting patient benefit using agreed measures. This would establish that muscle restoration improves health.

milestones.label: Lasting benefits across several causes of heart damage
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show lasting gains in survival and daily function, with less need for transplants or mechanical pumps, across several causes of severe damage. This would establish who benefits.

milestones.label: Long-term follow-up establishes muscle durability and delayed risks
milestones.explanation: Continued follow-up would have to track muscle durability, dangerous heart rhythms, tumors, unintended tissue growth and immune problems. This would reveal delayed harm or loss of benefit.

uncertain: How much new muscle is enough, and how mature and coordinated with the heart must it become?
What long-term burden of medicines to prevent immune rejection would be acceptable?
How large and lasting must patient benefits be to count as success?

page.title: Myocardial remuscularization in adult heart failure
page.definition: New cardiomyocytes, the heart's contractile cells, replace muscle lost from an adult heart. They can be injected into the ventricular wall or implanted as engineered tissue on its outer surface. The added muscle survives, contributes to contraction and improves patients' symptoms, activity or survival. A change in pumping function alone cannot establish that new muscle formed.

goal.need: Nearly 6.7 million US adults aged 20 or older have heart failure, which appeared on 452,573 US death certificates in 2023. Muscle replacement addresses a subset. After a heart attack, scar replaces muscle that once contracted. Medicines can improve symptoms and survival while that scar persists. For patients still limited by muscle loss, restoring contraction could improve exercise capacity and help some avoid a donor-heart transplant. With donor-cell grafts, the benefit must outweigh the risks of surgery and immunosuppression.

completion.title: FDA grants traditional approval to a myocardial replacement product for adult heart failure.
completion.criterion: FDA grants a biologics licence through traditional approval for a cell or tissue product that replaces myocardium in adults with heart failure. The product meets safety, purity, potency and substantial-evidence-of-effectiveness requirements. Traditional approval accepts clinical endpoints reflecting meaningful benefit or validated surrogate endpoints. For cardiac cell therapies, FDA generally recommends mortality or cardiovascular/heart-failure hospitalization endpoints for pivotal trials. No universal effect-size or follow-up cutoff is specified.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Frequently Asked Questions—Developing Potential Cellular and Gene Therapy Products, question 34; Cellular Therapy for Cardiac Disease, section VI.D.3.
completion.threshold_quote: there must be substantial evidence of effectiveness.
completion.basis: Traditional FDA licensure supplies a product-specific US benefit–risk decision. FDA's cardiac guidance excludes ejection fraction alone as a pivotal primary efficacy endpoint. Japan granted RiHEART, a donor-derived cardiomyocyte sheet, conditional marketing approval in March 2026 for severe ischemic heart failure inadequately responsive to standard treatment. The approval lasts seven years and requires postmarketing assessment. As of 25 November 2026, FDA's licensed-product list contains no myocardial replacement product for adult heart failure.

milestones.title: A myocardial replacement product shows biological activity and safety sufficient for human testing.
milestones.criterion: Before human testing, preclinical studies establish a scientific rationale for clinical use by demonstrating biological activity and an acceptable safety profile for the product and its intended delivery system. Study duration and safety assessments depend on the product and route.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Cellular Therapy for Cardiac Disease, section IV.A; nonbinding development guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: demonstrate an acceptable safety profile of your product and its delivery system.

milestones.title: An adult with heart failure receives replacement cardiomyocytes in an authorized early-phase trial.
milestones.criterion: Document administration of the investigational cell or tissue product to an adult who meets the trial's heart-failure eligibility criteria. BioVAT-HF specifies engineered muscle implantation for reduced ejection fraction of 35% or less and a ventricular segment with impaired movement. HEAL-CHF specifies intramyocardial cardiomyocyte injection during coronary bypass surgery.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a), defines the first-human-use stage. BioVAT-HF and HEAL-CHF specify the intervention and eligibility for their respective routes.
milestones.threshold_quote: initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans

milestones.title: Cardiomyocyte implantation improves 12-month six-minute walk distance versus bypass alone at P≤0.05.
milestones.criterion: In HEAL-CHF, compare the change from baseline in six-minute walk distance at 12 months between patients randomized to intramyocardial cardiomyocytes plus coronary bypass and those randomized to bypass alone. The difference must favor the cell group at two-sided P≤0.05. The protocol measures distance at 6 and 12 months as a secondary endpoint and sets no minimum gain in metres.
milestones.set_by: HELP Therapeutics, HEAL-CHF protocol version 6.2, 1 August 2021, sections 2.2.2 and 6.5.2; NCT03763136. This test was specified for injected cardiomyocytes accompanying bypass surgery.
milestones.threshold_quote: A two-sided p-value of ≤0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses.

milestones.title: A controlled pivotal trial establishes clinical benefit from myocardial replacement in heart failure.
milestones.criterion: A controlled phase 3 trial meets its prespecified efficacy criterion on a clinically relevant primary endpoint, generally mortality or cardiovascular/heart-failure hospitalization under FDA’s cardiac cell-therapy guidance. Controls receive standard care, and patients are followed for survival. FDA specifies no common effect size, sample size or follow-up duration. An ejection-fraction increase alone does not satisfy this stage.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Cellular Therapy for Cardiac Disease, sections VI.D.3–4, VI.E and VI.G; nonbinding development guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: endpoints such as mortality and cardiovascular or heart failure hospitalizations

milestones.title: Donor cardiomyocytes survive in the infarcted myocardium of a small animal.
milestones.criterion: After implantation in a small-animal model of myocardial infarction, tissue examination identifies surviving donor-derived cardiomyocytes in the treated ventricular region. Report the interval from implantation to examination.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Cellular Therapy for Cardiac Disease, section IV.B.2, on the use of small-animal models.
milestones.threshold_quote: survive and differentiate in the myocardium following infarction.

milestones.title: Donor cardiomyocytes persist as identifiable muscle in a treated human ventricle.
milestones.criterion: At follow-up, identify graft-derived cardiomyocytes in the treated ventricular region and report the interval since implantation. In an explanted heart, cardiac muscle staining can establish cell identity and donor-specific genetic variants can establish graft origin. Wall thickness alone cannot distinguish donor muscle from other tissue.
milestones.set_by: European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart, 2019 position paper, section on immunosuppression. The group requires durable engraftment without a fixed duration. BioVAT-HF demonstrates how graft identity can be tested.
milestones.threshold_quote: durable engraftment of the cells/graft is required

not_found: No common regenerated-muscle mass, ejection-fraction gain or follow-up cutoff defining completed remuscularization was found in FDA guidance, NHLBI priorities or the accessible trial protocols.
No controlled pivotal result establishing mortality or hospitalization benefit from implanted cardiomyocytes was found.
The NEJM publisher’s full text and accompanying protocol for the 2026 BioVAT-HF report were inaccessible; its PubMed abstract was accessible.
No cardiology society or regulator position opposing investigation of cardiomyocyte replacement itself was identified.

results.finding: Nude rats (n=15) had identifiable donor cardiomyocytes in viable epicardial grafts 4 weeks after implantation.
results.detail: Cardiac troponin T staining identified cardiomyocytes, and primate mitochondrial staining distinguished donor cells from rat cells.
results.quote:
rhesus macaque CMs could be identified 4 weeks after implantation of 
viable but not lethally irradiated EHM (Extended Data Fig. 2b).

results.finding: Among 20 implanted macaques completing follow-up, no arrhythmias or tumours were observed through up to 6 months.
results.detail: One high-dose macaque with heart failure died of low cardiac output during post-anaesthesia recovery. The study also recorded immunosuppression-related adverse effects and osteochondral foci in some grafts.
results.quote:
Importantly, no arrhythmia and tumour formation 
were observed in any of the EHM-implanted macaques (n = 20), which 
completed follow-up with 66 EHM patches implanted

results.finding: One adult with heart failure and baseline LVEF of 35% received an epicardial engineered heart muscle graft in BioVAT-HF.
results.detail: The Paul-Ehrlich-Institut and the competent ethics committee approved the trial.
results.quote:
Note that the heart is from a 
patient implanted with a mid-dose level EHM allograft (10x EHM; refer also to 
Fig. 5a, Extended Data Fig. 8d).

results.finding: Donor-derived cardiomyocytes persisted in the treated ventricular region of one BioVAT-HF patient at about 3 months.
results.quote:
Allele distribution of 7 distinct SNVs showed the presence of iPSC-derived 
alleles in biopsies of the patched area.

results.finding: BioVAT-HF implanted engineered heart muscle in 20 eligible adults with heart failure.
results.quote: A total of 20 patients were treated in the study.

results.finding: In 12 BioVAT recipients at 3 months, treated ventricular wall thickness increased by 4.5 mm.
results.detail: One patient underwent heart transplantation. The supplied text gives no tissue examination result for the explanted heart.
results.quote: The least-squares mean increase in the target-wall thickness was 4.5 mm (90% confidence interval [CI], 3.7 to 5.4; P<0.001)

results.finding: In HEAL-CHF, 10 of 20 randomized patients with advanced ischemic heart failure received intramyocardial cardiomyocytes during bypass surgery.
results.detail: HEAL-CHF was registered as NCT03763136. Both randomized groups underwent bypass surgery.
results.quote: all 10 patients in this group developed accelerated idioventricular rhythm, typically emerging 5 to 7 days post-transplantation.

results.finding: In HEAL-CHF (n=20 randomized), six-minute walk distance improved significantly more with cardiomyocyte injection plus bypass than with bypass alone.
results.detail: The 12-month timing in the abstract is attached to a separate list of outcomes.
results.quote: Secondary efficacy analyses indicated that cell transplantation provided significantly greater improvements in 6-min walk distance

results.finding: Intramyocardially injected human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes formed viable grafts at 12 weeks in a rhesus infarction study (n=16).
results.detail: The 12-week cohort comprised six cell recipients and four vehicle controls. All animals received immunosuppression. The study used a single dose at reperfusion in an acute infarction model.
results.quote: Subsequently, at week 12 after cell transplantation, immunofluorescence staining of hcTnI identified the viable hiPSC-CM grafts in the monkey myocardium.

results.finding: After intramyocardial injection of human iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes in infarcted rats, ejection fraction rose 18.86% relative to baseline (9 treated and 8 control rats analyzed).
results.detail: The ejection-fraction change is relative to the treated group's own baseline. The longer tumorigenicity assessment used subcutaneous injections in nude mice.
results.quote: In the iPSC-CM injection group, the ejection fraction improved by 18.86% (from 44.09 to 52.41%), and fractional shortening improved by 23.69% (from 23.08 to 28.54%).

results.finding: In swine with heart failure (n = 20), injected cardiac spheroids improved ejection fraction versus hydrogel alone (p = 0.002).
results.detail: The MRI groups included 8 spheroid-treated, 7 hydrogel-only and 5 sham swine. The ejection fraction difference versus sham was not statistically significant. Most grafted cells had disappeared by week 8.
results.quote: Only CS-transplanted swine exhibited improved EF (p = 0.001 [CS vs. GH: p = 0.002, CS vs. sham: p = 0.074])

results.finding: Histology identified surviving human donor cardiomyocytes in infarcted NOG mouse hearts 6 months after intramyocardial injection (follow-up cohort n=5).
results.detail: The paper reports 5 mice in the long-term follow-up cohort. It does not specify how many of those hearts contributed to the 6-month histology.
results.quote: In summary, the engrafted iPSC-CMs survived at least 6 months after injection and proliferated well during the first month, but gradually lost their proliferation capacity, which resulted in mature and non-proliferative CMs at 6 months ( Fig. 6c ).

results.finding: Histology identified surviving human donor cardiomyocytes in epicardial grafts in all five infarcted rats examined one month after implantation.
results.detail: Grafts stained for human β1 integrin and contained β-myosin heavy chain-positive cardiomyocytes. A thin fibrotic layer typically separated the graft from the host myocardium.
results.quote: one month after implantation, grafts consisted of densely packed living human CMs that showed limited sarcomere alignment

definition = "New cardiomyocytes, the heart's contractile cells, replace muscle lost from an adult heart. They can be injected into the ventricular wall or implanted as engineered tissue on its outer surface. The added muscle survives, contributes to contraction and improves patients' symptoms, activity or survival. A change in pumping function alone cannot establish that new muscle formed.". Reason: The definition needs to distinguish surviving replacement muscle from functional changes that transplanted cells can produce through other mechanisms.

goal.need = "Nearly 6.7 million US adults aged 20 or older have heart failure, which appeared on 452,573 US death certificates in 2023. Muscle replacement addresses a subset. After a heart attack, scar replaces muscle that once contracted. Medicines can improve symptoms and survival while that scar persists. For patients still limited by muscle loss, restoring contraction could improve exercise capacity and help some avoid a donor-heart transplant. With donor-cell grafts, the benefit must outweigh the risks of surgery and immunosuppression.". Reason: The current paragraph gives the overall burden but omits what medicines leave untreated and what successful muscle replacement could change for patients.

add statement by European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart, 2019: "further scrutinize the possibility to regenerate the failing heart by remuscularization". Reason: The working group's position paper names remuscularization more specifically than the existing multi-organ research priority.

add not found: "No cardiology society or regulator position opposing investigation of cardiomyocyte replacement itself was identified.". Reason: Published criticism of earlier cardiac cell therapies does not establish professional opposition to replacing lost cardiomyocytes.

edit completion: basis = "Traditional FDA licensure supplies a product-specific US benefit\u2013risk decision. FDA's cardiac guidance excludes ejection fraction alone as a pivotal primary efficacy endpoint. Japan granted RiHEART, a donor-derived cardiomyocyte sheet, conditional marketing approval in March 2026 for severe ischemic heart failure inadequately responsive to standard treatment. The approval lasts seven years and requires postmarketing assessment. As of 25 November 2026, FDA's licensed-product list contains no myocardial replacement product for adult heart failure."; refs = [4, 5, 6, 15, 17]. Reason: Japan's conditional authorization of a cardiomyocyte sheet is a concrete regulatory near miss that the US licensure basis omits.
add case "Epicardial tissue implantation". Reason: BioVAT-HF tests engineered muscle attached to the heart surface.
add case "Intramyocardial cell injection". Reason: HEAL-CHF tests cells injected into the ventricular muscle during bypass surgery.

add milestone after None: "Donor cardiomyocytes survive in the infarcted myocardium of a small animal.". Reason: The sequence currently begins at readiness for human testing and skips the small-animal demonstration of graft survival after infarction.

edit m1: criterion = "Before human testing, preclinical studies establish a scientific rationale for clinical use by demonstrating biological activity and an acceptable safety profile for the product and its intended delivery system. Study duration and safety assessments depend on the product and route.". Reason: The macaque counts, outcomes and adverse event belong in the evidence for human testing rather than in the preclinical test itself.

edit m2: title = "An adult with heart failure receives replacement cardiomyocytes in an authorized early-phase trial."; criterion = "Document administration of the investigational cell or tissue product to an adult who meets the trial's heart-failure eligibility criteria. BioVAT-HF specifies engineered muscle implantation for reduced ejection fraction of 35% or less and a ventricular segment with impaired movement. HEAL-CHF specifies intramyocardial cardiomyocyte injection during coronary bypass surgery."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a), defines the first-human-use stage. BioVAT-HF and HEAL-CHF specify the intervention and eligibility for their respective routes."; set_by_kind = "regulator"; threshold_quote = "initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans"; threshold_ref = 16; refs = [16, 13, 8, 9, 10]. Reason: Initial human administration is a distinct stage for both routes, and the present criterion mixes that stage with graft histology and interim outcomes.

add milestone after m2: "Donor cardiomyocytes persist as identifiable muscle in a treated human ventricle.". Reason: Administering a product and demonstrating that its donor cardiomyocytes survive in a human heart are separate achievements.

edit m3: criterion = "In HEAL-CHF, compare the change from baseline in six-minute walk distance at 12 months between patients randomized to intramyocardial cardiomyocytes plus coronary bypass and those randomized to bypass alone. The difference must favor the cell group at two-sided P\u22640.05. The protocol measures distance at 6 and 12 months as a secondary endpoint and sets no minimum gain in metres.". Reason: The criterion should retain the trial's statistical comparison and identify its exploratory status without including observed outcomes or adverse events.
